outcome: On 8 Sep 2026 OpenAI announced an AI-produced, Lean-formalised manuscript claiming finite-time blow-up of the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations under a smooth external force (Clay alternatives C on R³ and D on the torus), which no qualified referee has accepted and which the Clay Institute says has ‘apparently been settled’ but has not adjudicated; the unforced questions (Clay A and B) are untouched by it and remain open, and several unrefereed unforced-regularity claims from 2025–2026 have drawn no public engagement.
problem_asks: The bullet is only the title: ‘Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness’. Unpacked from the Clay formulation as the Wikipedia article states it (the Clay PDF itself was unreadable to me): (A) on R³, for smooth divergence-free initial velocity of finite energy and zero external force, do smooth globally defined solutions of the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations exist for all time? (B) the same question on the periodic torus T³ with zero force. (C) on R³: is there at least one set of smooth initial data and smooth external force (finite energy throughout) for which no globally smooth solution exists, i.e. a finite-time breakdown? (D) the periodic-torus analogue of C. The Clay prize is for resolving one of A–D. The bullet does not say which alternative it means, so all four are listed and the choice is left to the judging pass.

events.what_happened: OpenAI announced on 8 Sep 2026 a claimed proof, produced by an internal multi-agent system, that the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations have finite-time blow-up from smooth finite-energy data at rest under a smooth external force, for every positive viscosity, on R³ (Clay C) and on the periodic torus R³/Z³ (Clay D). It came with a manuscript titled ‘Finite time blowup for Navier–Stokes’ (166 pages, on cdn.openai.com) and a Lean 4 formalisation at github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler, described in its README as ‘Lean certificates accompanying Navier-Stokes and Euler results’. OpenAI said it would not claim the Clay prize. I could not read OpenAI’s own announcement (openai.com returned 403) or the manuscript PDF (returned as binary), so the mathematical content is known from the repository README (read through a fetch), the critiques below, Wikipedia’s account of the announcement, and press reports.
events.revisions: Manuscript and repository reported as released 8 Sep 2026 in all sources read. The GitHub page shows 2 commits on main, with no dates. Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen (arXiv 2610.08144 §3) cite Lean commit f9e8bc5; a reference list quoted in a search result cites commit 8937a8f4… (not opened); these may be different snapshots. Page count is 166 in citing arXiv papers, but a secondary report says roughly 100 pages. A self-published LaTeX reconstruction of the 166-page PDF appeared 20 Sep 2026 (zenodo 22852310). No revised OpenAI version was found.
events.delivers: If the claim holds: for the forced 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations there are smooth external forces and smooth finite-energy data (data at rest, kinetic energy uniformly bounded along the solution) for which the solution ceases to be smooth in finite time, both on R³ (alternative C) and on the periodic torus (alternative D), for every positive viscosity, per the README. Restrictions: the force is smooth and, per Cao–Chi–Nie and a search-result summary of the announcement, compactly supported in space; the result is a breakdown statement for forced flows only; it says nothing about zero force.
events.remains: Global smoothness of unforced flows on R³ (alternative A) and on T³ (alternative B). Wikipedia, the Clay page and every source read say these remain open, and no source claims otherwise. Also open: whether the Lean statements match the natural-language theorem, which is disputed (see doubts).

events.directly_checkable: The Lean development, rebuildable with lake build per the README. The Lean statement can be read for what it asserts (forced blow-up, alternatives C and D). Whether it matches the natural-language argument is not checkable by a non-specialist, and the README does not say whether sorry or extra axioms are used (not read). The geometry question in Duraiswami’s abstract is a concrete check: that abstract states the cone condition needs radii of order 10^20.
events.doubts: (1) Lean-to-natural-language fidelity. Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen (arXiv 2610.08144 §3, opened) report that the natural-language argument for Lemma 8.6 uses m+4 derivatives (their equation (8.19)) while the Lean estimate uses m+5, so the NL paper claims a stronger inverse estimate than the cited Lean formalisation. They also report that the NL bound for estimate (10.19) depends only on B_R while the Lean bound also depends on A_R, which they describe as a change of argument, not only of constant. They say they did not check compilation, sorry or axioms. (2) Geometry of the construction. Duraiswami (arXiv 2609.17642, abstract read) argues that the GD1998 swirl geometry does not recast into the similarity variables as stated, that the Dirichlet axis problem has no resolution-stable solution, that a core symmetric about the dividing plane cannot meet the moment identities, and that the cone condition needs radii of order 10^20. Single author; not checked against the full paper or code. (3) Scope restriction, not an error. Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol (arXiv 2609.20803, abstract read) prove regularity at the putative singular point under real-analytic forcing and two properties they attribute to the OpenAI construction. Their abstract says that for such constructions the force cannot vanish identically near the singular point or be real-analytic in space. Wikipedia reads this as also excluding extension to A and B; the abstract itself does not say so. (4) No peer review and no journal acceptance found. (5) Scientific American (8 Oct 2026, opened) reports that three papers in OpenAI’s 6 Oct release were withdrawn after experts found significant errors. It does not name them, so whether this manuscript is one of them is not established. (6) A secondary search summary says the Association for Human Mathematics statement holds the natural-language Navier–Stokes proof already wrong. The AHM statement I read (on Tao’s blog, opened) does not say this, so I treat that claim as unverified.
events.direction: Claims breakdown. In Clay’s terms it answers alternatives C and D in the affirmative: there exist smooth data and smooth forces with no globally smooth solution. It says nothing about unforced flows, which are alternatives A and B.
events.object: A smooth divergence-free initial velocity field at rest with finite energy, plus a smooth external force, for every positive viscosity, whose solution develops unbounded velocity in finite time while kinetic energy stays uniformly bounded (repository README: smooth data and forcing on R³ with no global smooth solution; the analogue on R³/Z³ for D). Per Duraiswami’s reading of the construction, the solution is an axisymmetric swirl core in similarity-type variables. Whether the object is explicit or an existence argument for an approximate profile with a stability argument is not established from any source I could read.

One source dates the posting to 7 Sep 2026 and another to 8 Sep. The Euler result is axisymmetric with swirl, with a force smooth in space and time up to the blow-up time (secondary description). The IPM result was later posted on arXiv as event buckmaster-alpoge-coiculescu-ipm-arxiv-2026-09-15. Quanta reports the Euler proof was Lean-verified by 22 Aug 2026 and the first Boussinesq blow-up solution was found on 15 Aug (the latter from a secondary account of their AI statement). Tao is reported to have praised the work (secondary; a 7 Sep post was not on his blog front page when I read it).

A secondary search summary says the statement also says he and Alpöge believe they have blow-up for hypo-dissipative Navier–Stokes but will not release it because Lean verification is incomplete and no writeup exists. I did not read that sentence in the statement itself.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2609.10262 (Cao, Chi, Nie), ‘Density of Forces Producing Navier–Stokes Blowup’, submitted 9 Sep 2026. Starting from OpenAI’s compact forced blow-up solution, it constructs a blow-up solution near every given smooth solution while preserving its initial velocity. The result is that, for fixed viscosity and zero initial velocity, smooth forces that make the 3D Navier–Stokes equations lose classical regularity by a prescribed time are dense in the relative L¹_t H^s_x topology on the torus and on R³ exactly when s < 1/2.
events.revisions: v1 9 Sep 2026; v2 11 Sep 2026 withdrawn (1 KB); v3 21 Sep 2026; v4 22 Sep 2026 (abstract metadata updated, ‘manuscript unchanged’).
events.delivers: Density of forcing terms that produce breakdown for forced 3D Navier–Stokes, on the torus and on R³, for s < 1/2. It depends wholly on OpenAI’s forced construction.
events.remains: The unforced problem (A and B) and the Clay alternatives beyond this forced breakdown class. It takes OpenAI’s construction as given.
events.doubts: Inherits every doubt about the OpenAI construction, because it begins from it (see the OpenAI event).

withdrawn.what: v2 (1 KB) was withdrawn on 11 Sep 2026. v3 and v4 restored the paper, with v4 described as ‘manuscript unchanged’ with abstract metadata updated.

events.object: Forcing terms, dense in the stated topology, for which the forced 3D Navier–Stokes equations lose classical regularity, built near any given smooth solution while preserving its initial velocity.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2609.17642 (Duraiswami), ‘Self-similar swirl between contracting porous walls: the GD1998 exact Navier–Stokes solution revisited in the similarity variables of the OpenAI 2026 forced blow-up construction’, submitted 15 Sep 2026 (31 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables). Abstract read. It argues that the GD1998 boundary-value problem does not recast into the similarity variables as stated; that the Dirichlet axis problem has no resolution-stable solution, so the core must be posed as a Cauchy problem from the axis; that a core symmetric about the dividing plane cannot meet the moment identities; that the cone condition is Rayleigh’s criterion with axial shear and needs radii of order 10^20; and that a non-symmetric core meets the moment identities to 0.2%. It also says that the forced theorem, and this study, leave the unforced equations as they were.
events.delivers: No blow-up result. It claims specific obstructions to the geometry the OpenAI forced construction is said to rest on, and proposes a laboratory chamber as an experiment.
events.remains: Everything in the Clay statement. The author does not address the unforced problem.

checked_by.what_they_did: Re-analysed the swirl-core setup of the forced construction in the similarity variables and reported obstructions (abstract read)

events.directly_checkable: The author reports a computable obstruction (a cone condition needing radii of order 10^20) that can be checked from the construction's stated parameters, not read here.
events.doubts: Abstract-only reading. The author’s own report says that at moderate inflow and strong swirl the spectrum does not converge in axial resolution, and leaves this open. Not checked against the full paper or code.
events.direction: Against the geometry of the OpenAI forced construction as the author reads it. Not about unforced flows.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2609.20803 (Constantin, Ignatova, Vicol), ‘Regularity of asymptotically axisymmetric solutions to the 3D Navier–Stokes equations with analytic forcing’, v1 17 Sep 2026, v2 29 Sep 2026. The abstract says OpenAI ‘has recently announced a proof of finite time singularity formation’ for a C∞ body force and identifies two features of that construction: (i) the angular mean satisfies anisotropic Type II bounds, and (ii) the solution is exactly axisymmetric in a collapsing core. They consider real-analytic forcing, assume (i) and (ii), and prove the solutions are regular at the putative singular point. The abstract also says that for constructions with (i), (ii) and a force bounded in C² up to the singular time, the force ‘can neither vanish identically near the singular point’ nor be real-analytic in space.
events.delivers: Conditional regularity: under real-analytic forcing and assumptions (i) and (ii), solutions are regular at the putative singular point. As a corollary, a construction with (i), (ii) and force bounded in C² up to the singular time cannot have a force that vanishes identically near the singular point or is real-analytic in space.
events.remains: The OpenAI class of smooth but non-analytic forces is not excluded except as the corollary states. The unforced problem (A, B) and the forced breakdown without these assumptions are untouched.

events.what_happened: Zenodo 22820521 (Santibañez-Leal), ‘An independent audit of the September 2026 fluid blowup claims, and a trade-off between force regularity and dissipation’, published 17 Sep 2026, version 0.01 (a newer version exists). It audits the Alpöge–Buckmaster claims (2D inviscid Boussinesq and 3D Euler with smooth forcing) and the OpenAI claims (forced 3D Navier–Stokes at every positive viscosity, and unforced Euler). It rebuilt and replayed the OpenAI Lean certificate through the Lean kernel, validated a reduced amplitude model against pseudospectral simulation, and re-derived a published hypodissipative threshold (22−8√7)/9. It reports that controlling one derivative of the force caps the exponent at 1/480 for a published smooth-forcing schedule, and it records a dated prediction about an unreleased hypodissipative sequel. Landing page read; the abstract’s key sentences were quoted by the fetch.
events.revisions: Version 0.01 read; a newer version exists (not read)
events.delivers: Its own statement: it does not prove blow-up for any equation. It establishes that the OpenAI Lean development replays through the Lean kernel, and that the reduction gives a 1/480 exponent cap under its stated assumptions. It does not verify the mathematics of either announced proof.
events.remains: The mathematics of both announced proofs. The unforced Navier–Stokes problem is outside its scope.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2609.23868 (Petrillo, Glimm), ‘The Positive Defect Problem: Target and Admissibility Criteria for a Programmatic Search for Unforced Navier–Stokes Blowup’, submitted 20 Sep 2026. Abstract read. It says the unforced problem, statements (A) and (B), remains open and proposes a target for a programmatic search: a positive defect (energy loss on a finite time window for a Leray–Hopf solution from smooth periodic data). It proves that a positive defect implies blow-up and so a negative answer to statement (B); the converse is not known. It reports a pseudo-spectral search at 128³ and 256³. It states that every implication not marked otherwise is a Lean 4 theorem over Mathlib, and that the library contains no Navier–Stokes object. The abstract also says that on 7 and 8 Sep 2026 ‘programmatic search produced singularities’, including a forced Navier–Stokes singularity at every fixed viscosity.
events.delivers: Conditional implications: a positive defect implies blow-up on the torus and so a negative answer to (B). Machine-checked as Lean implications, per the abstract, but the Lean library has no Navier–Stokes object, so the implications are not formal statements about Navier–Stokes.
events.remains: Statements (A) and (B) remain open. The positive-defect property is a target, not a result.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 over Mathlib (for the stated implications only, per the abstract)

events.doubts: The positive-defect property is not shown to hold for any solution. The Lean development covers implications rather than Navier–Stokes itself, per the abstract. The abstract’s characterisation of the 7–8 Sep results as products of ‘programmatic search’ is the authors’ own and is not explained.
events.direction: Conditional implication toward a negative answer to (B). No unforced singularity found.

events.what_happened: arXiv (Ganeshram, Duruisseaux, Anandkumar), ‘Self-Similar Singularity of the Euler Equations on R³’, submitted 9 Sep 2026, revised 24 Sep 2026, 111 pages. Abstract read. It gives numerical and computer-assisted evidence of a self-similar finite-time singularity in 3D Euler on the unbounded domain at blow-up rate 0.5, using a physics-informed neural network with a self-similar ansatz, represented with splines. It sets up a stability framework that reduces nonlinear stability to a large but finite collection of explicit estimates and computable constants, and the abstract does not say whether that framework is complete.
events.delivers: Numerical evidence for a self-similar blow-up of 3D Euler on R³. Does not prove a singularity.
events.remains: A proof of blow-up for Euler; all Navier–Stokes alternatives.
events.doubts: Numerical evidence. The stability framework’s completion is not stated in the abstract.
events.direction: Toward a singularity for the inviscid Euler equations (numerical). Neighbouring, not the Clay problem.
events.object: An approximate self-similar singular profile for 3D Euler on R³ at blow-up rate 0.5, found with a physics-informed neural network and represented with splines (abstract).

events.what_happened: arXiv 2610.08144 (Bastounis, Circelli, Hansen), ‘Navier–Stokes lost in translation: Why Lean verification of AI autoformalisation does not guarantee correct natural language proofs’, submitted 6 Oct 2026, v1 only. Read from the arXiv abstract and §1, §3 (HTML). It analyses OpenAI’s announced Navier–Stokes and Euler manuscripts against their Lean repository. Example 3.1 (‘The NL paper claims a stronger inverse estimate than the cited Lean formalisation’) concerns Lemma 8.6 and its equation (8.19), which uses m+4 derivatives where the Lean estimate uses m+5. Example 3.3 concerns estimate (10.19): the NL bound depends only on B_R whereas the Lean estimate also depends on A_R, a change of argument rather than of constant. They state they make no claim about the correctness of OpenAI’s natural-language proof.
events.delivers: Establishes, for the specific examples in §3, that the Lean development does not in every place establish the natural-language statement: in Example 3.1 the NL claim is stronger than the cited Lean estimate; in Example 3.3 the Lean bound is structured differently. Argues more generally that faithful translation from natural-language mathematics to Lean is hard.
events.remains: Whether the natural-language proof is correct. Whether the Lean theorem statements match the intended forced C and D claims in full, which the examples do not settle. Whether OpenAI has revised the manuscript (not found).

checked_by.who: Alexander Bastounis, Fabian Circelli, Anders C. Hansen
checked_by.qualification: Affiliations not on the arXiv page (secondary: King’s College London; Cambridge, not verified)
checked_by.what_they_did: Compared the NL manuscript and Lean code at named lemmas and estimates; reported mismatches; disclaimed a verdict on NL correctness

events.directly_checkable: Example 3.1 and Example 3.3 can be checked by comparing Lemma 8.6 and (10.19) of the manuscript with the Lean estimates named in §3.
events.doubts: The examples are specific and were not checked against the full repository by me. The paper’s broader complexity-theoretic claim (Solvability Complexity Index hierarchy, harder than the Halting problem) is not evaluated here. Compilation and sorry are not addressed in the paper.
events.direction: Against the claim that the Lean development certifies the natural-language argument at these points. Neutral on the truth of the theorem.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2509.25116 (Hou, Wang, Yang), ‘Nonuniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions to the unforced incompressible 3D Navier–Stokes Equation’, v1 29 Sep 2025, v2 19 Mar 2026. Abstract read. It claims ‘to our knowledge, the first rigorous computer-assisted proof demonstrating such nonuniqueness’. The argument constructs a self-similar Leray–Hopf solution, decomposes the linearised operator into a coercive part plus a compact perturbation approximated by a finite-rank operator, and verifies by computer that the restricted operator is invertible, which certifies an unstable eigenpair and hence a second solution. The abstract says this yields infinitely many Leray–Hopf solutions. Hou talks on it were given at ENS Paris (7 Apr 2026) and Cambridge (10 Apr 2026) according to secondary listings.
events.revisions: v1 29 Sep 2025; v2 19 Mar 2026 (no change of date shown for the first public argument)
events.delivers: Non-uniqueness of Leray–Hopf (weak) solutions to the unforced 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, from the same data, with infinitely many solutions, by a computer-assisted argument. The abstract does not say whether the second solutions are smooth or singular.
events.remains: The Clay statement, as read through Wikipedia and Clay’s summary, is about existence and smoothness, not uniqueness. Smoothness and breakdown questions (A to D) are not addressed.
events.directly_checkable: Computer-assisted (rigorous numerical certification, not Lean). The certified steps are the invertibility check on the restricted operator and the existence of the unstable eigenpair; neither was checked by me.
events.doubts: No journal reference on the arXiv page. The computer-assisted code and error bounds are not confirmed as released in the abstract. Talk listings are presentations, not refereeing.
events.direction: Cuts against uniqueness for unforced Leray–Hopf weak solutions. Its bearing on existence and smoothness of smooth solutions is not stated in the abstract.
events.object: A self-similar Leray–Hopf solution of the unforced 3D Navier–Stokes equations whose linearisation has a certified unstable eigenpair, giving a second Leray–Hopf solution; the computer-assisted certification is what establishes the eigenpair.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2508.19590 (Myong-Hwan Ri), ‘Global regularity of Leray–Hopf weak solutions to 3D Navier–Stokes equations’, submitted 27 Aug 2025, v1 only, 17 pages. Abstract read (the rendering is OCR-garbled in places). It claims that any Leray–Hopf weak solution to the 3D Navier–Stokes equations with initial data in H^{1/2}(R³) is regular, in L^∞(0,∞; H^{1/2}), using a supercritical space whose norm is compared with the homogeneous H^{1/2} norm, energy estimates for high-frequency parts, and a rescaling argument.
events.delivers: If correct: global regularity of unforced 3D Navier–Stokes on R³ for Leray–Hopf solutions with H^{1/2} data. Restrictions: R³ only; data class H^{1/2}; unforced. Whether this class includes the smooth finite-energy data of Clay A is not stated on the page. Smooth finite-energy data lie in H^{1/2}, so it appears to, but I have not checked this.
events.remains: The torus (B), and the forced breakdown alternatives (C, D). No restriction is needed for A if the class inclusion holds.
events.doubts: Unrefereed single-version arXiv preprint with no journal reference. No expert engagement found in about 13 months. No specific error identified by anyone. I read only the abstract, not the proof, so I have not checked any step.
events.direction: Would establish global regularity for the unforced problem on R³ for H^{1/2} data, if correct.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2601.15685 (Ri), ‘Global regularity for the Navier–Stokes equations with application to global solvability for the Euler equations’, submitted 22 Jan 2026, v1 only. Abstract read as a paraphrase by the fetch: for d ≥ 3 and initial data in H^s(R^d) with s ≥ −1 + d/2, Leray–Hopf weak solutions remain in L^∞(0,∞; H^s) and are therefore globally regular, using a supercritical norm with an inverse-logarithmic weight in frequency and rescaling to obtain viscosity-independent bounds. The title’s Euler application is not described in the abstract.
events.delivers: If correct: global regularity of unforced Navier–Stokes on R^d for d ≥ 3 with H^s data, s ≥ −1 + d/2 (for d = 3, s ≥ 1/2). It does not address the torus. It overlaps the 2025 Ri claim at d = 3.
events.remains: The torus (B) and the forced alternatives (C, D).
events.doubts: Unrefereed single-version arXiv preprint with no journal reference. No engagement found. No specific error identified. Only the abstract page was read.
events.direction: Would establish global regularity for the unforced problem on R^d (d ≥ 3) for H^s data, if correct.

events.what_happened: Zenodo 15801528 (Andrei Polozov), ‘Global Regularity for the 3D Incompressible Navier–Stokes Equations via Emergent Nonlinear Vorticity Dissipation’, published 3 Jul 2025 (modified 4 Jul 2025), v1, CC BY 4.0. Landing page read. It claims global existence, smoothness and uniqueness for smooth divergence-free data with no forcing, on the whole space and on the periodic domain, with no smallness, symmetry or decay assumptions, and calls the work ‘a complete and self-contained resolution of the global regularity problem’.
events.delivers: Claims unforced global existence and smoothness on R³ and on the torus (Clay A and B) if correct.
events.remains: Forced breakdown (C, D), and any unforced claim that is not established by the argument.
events.doubts: Self-published Zenodo record with no peer review, and no formal verification or expert validation mentioned. The landing page gives only the abstract; the PDF was not read. The claim that all known blow-up mechanisms are excluded is asserted, not shown in what I read.
events.direction: Claims unforced regularity on both R³ and the torus (A and B), if correct.
people: Andrei Polozov (Cégep de Sainte-Foy; project leader per the record)

events.what_happened: Zenodo 16991818 (Anna Paseva, Global Institute of Logic and Cybernetics), ‘Comprehensive Resolutions of the Navier–Stokes Global Regularity Problem: Seven Independent Proofs’, published 29 Aug 2025, v1, CC BY 4.0. Landing page read. It claims seven independent proofs of global existence and smoothness for 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes, using a range of frameworks (harmonic analysis, critical Besov spaces, Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg theory, stochastic Lagrangian methods, and others), and says each is supported by ‘formalization sketches in Coq or Lean’. It says all results prove the absence of finite-time singularities under smooth data.
events.delivers: Claims unforced global existence and smoothness if correct. It is not stated to cover the torus.
events.remains: Forced breakdown (C, D), and any part of the seven arguments not established by the record.
events.doubts: Seven claimed independent proofs in one unreviewed Zenodo preprint. The formalisations are described as sketches, not completed checks. The 327.5 kB PDF was not read.
events.direction: Claims unforced global regularity if correct.

NOT OPENED: the Preprints.org page returned 403, and the claim comes from a search snippet only.

events.what_happened: Thomas Hou (Caltech), talk ‘Recent progress on potential singularity of the 3D Navier–Stokes equation and related models’, Berkeley AMS seminar, 2 Apr 2025 (abstract opened). The abstract reports numerical evidence that 3D Navier–Stokes develops potentially singular behaviour at the origin with maximum vorticity growing by a factor of 10^7, induced by a potential finite-time singularity of 3D Euler. It also reports numerical evidence of tornado-like self-similar blow-up for a generalised axisymmetric Navier–Stokes equation with time-dependent fractional dimension (factor 10^21), and reviews computer-assisted work on 3D Euler with boundary. No write-up for the Navier–Stokes numerics was found, so the date is the talk date.
events.delivers: Numerical evidence only. The abstract says the Navier–Stokes behaviour is numerical and not a proof.
events.remains: Everything in the Clay statement.
events.doubts: Numerical. The abstract says so explicitly.
events.direction: Toward potential singularity for Navier–Stokes, numerically.
events.object: Numerical vorticity growth factor 10^7 at the origin for 3D Navier–Stokes, induced by a potential Euler singularity; plus a fractional-dimension axisymmetric numerical blow-up with growth factor 10^21 (abstract).

events.what_happened: arXiv 2509.14185 (Wang, Bennani, Martens, Racanière, … Buckmaster, Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Jiang, Lai; 22 authors including Google DeepMind researchers), ‘Discovery of Unstable Singularities’, submitted 17 Sep 2025, v1 only, 20 pages. Abstract read. It reports the first systematic discovery of new families of unstable self-similar singularities for the incompressible porous media equation and for the 3D Euler equation with boundary. It discusses boundary-free Euler and Navier–Stokes only as motivating open cases, and gives an empirical formula linking blow-up rate to order of instability. Accuracy is near double-float machine precision, which the abstract says meets the requirements for computer-assisted proof, which it does not claim to have been done.
events.revisions: v1 only; supplementary material said to follow in a later version
events.delivers: Numerical discovery of unstable self-similar singularity profiles for IPM and bounded 3D Euler with boundary. Not Navier–Stokes.
events.remains: Boundary-free Euler and all Navier–Stokes alternatives.
events.doubts: Numerical. The abstract says the Navier–Stokes case is only hypothesised.
events.direction: Toward singularities for neighbouring equations, numerically. Not Navier–Stokes.
events.object: Families of numerically computed unstable self-similar blow-up profiles for IPM and for 3D Euler with boundary, with an empirical blow-up-rate formula (abstract).
people: Google DeepMind collaborators (22 authors in total)

events.what_happened: arXiv 2407.06776 (Córdoba, Martínez-Zoroa, Zheng), ‘Finite time blow-up for the hypodissipative Navier Stokes equations with a force in L¹_t C^{1,ε}_x ∩ L^∞_t L²_x’, submitted 9 Jul 2024, v2 5 Aug 2024, 33 pages. Abstract read. For dissipation |∇|^α with α in [0, α0), α0 = (22−8√7)/9 ≈ 0.093, it constructs classical finite-energy solutions of forced fractional Navier–Stokes on R³×[0,T] whose time-integrated gradient norm diverges as t tends to T.
events.delivers: Finite-time blow-up for forced hypodissipative fractional Navier–Stokes on R³ with dissipation exponent α < α0. A changed version: fractional dissipation, forced, R³ only.
events.remains: Classical dissipation (α = 2), the unforced problem, and the torus.
events.doubts: None specific. The threshold α0 is the one the Santibañez-Leal audit re-derives.
events.direction: Forced blow-up for a changed dissipation. Neighbouring.
events.object: Classical finite-energy solutions of forced hypodissipative fractional Navier–Stokes on R³×[0,T], smooth for t below T, with the time integral of the gradient norm diverging at T (abstract).

events.what_happened: arXiv 2410.22920 (Córdoba, Martínez-Zoroa), ‘Finite time singularities of smooth solutions for the 2D incompressible porous media (IPM) equation with a smooth source’, submitted 30 Oct 2024; v3 13 Feb 2025 (minor corrections). Abstract read. Establishes smooth finite-energy solutions to 2D IPM with a compactly supported uniformly smooth source that develop singularities in finite time.

Abstract read. It proves finite-time, nearly self-similar blow-up of 2D Boussinesq and 3D axisymmetric Euler from smooth finite-energy data in a domain with boundary. A search summary reports the computer-assisted version was published in PNAS on 27 Jun 2025 (DOI 10.1073/pnas.2500940122); this was not opened.

It builds unforced 3D Euler singularities from infinitely many vorticity regions separated by vortex-free regions, not from self-similar coordinates, with the stated function-space regularity for times before the singularity. Published in Annals of PDE 11, article 19 (2025) per a search summary; not opened.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2609.26790 (Cheskidov, Dai, Palasek), ‘Cascade mechanisms for Navier–Stokes blow-up’, submitted 22 Sep 2026, v1 only. Abstract read. Works in the Obukhov dyadic shell model and a mixed Desnyansky–Novikov–Obukhov model rather than 3D Navier–Stokes. It claims an instantaneous Type I blow-up for the Obukhov model, a finite-time blow-up for the mixed model (Type II by a small margin), and a similar cascade at lower regularity for the inviscid system. It builds on the authors’ earlier preprint on an inverse energy cascade for 3D Navier–Stokes.

Abstract read. Commentary, not a mathematical result. It argues that the OpenAI output is a machine-checked certificate without a human-readable demonstration, and that accepting such proofs without human understanding shifts authority over truth.

disputes.summary: Buckmaster and Alpöge say OpenAI’s effort followed information about their work; OpenAI says its effort began on 1 Sep after hearing a rumour, and that its internal review found Buckmaster’s Codex prompts could not have influenced the system (10 Sep); its 13 Sep statement says no user inputs past 3 July could have influenced it, and Codex use before 3 July is not addressed. Alpöge disputes OpenAI’s independence, saying its proof looks more like another Euler blow-up proof they had. OpenAI credits Buckmaster and Alpöge with priority for the forced 3D Euler result while claiming the Navier–Stokes result (Quanta). Bubeck calls the allegations ‘false and inflammatory’ (secondary).

OpenAI’s 8 Sep statement says ‘while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models’ (quoted in the Wikipedia priority article and in a secondary search summary). Mark Chen is quoted as saying no one or no AI system searched user data to solve the problem. Buckmaster says he was told the model did not look up user data and got no answer on training.

The Clay Institute’s primary wording is that the problem has ‘apparently been settled’, with evaluation ‘deliberately unhurried’. Its problem page is marked ‘Active’ (opened). Wikipedia’s infobox says ‘(solution claimed)’. Some secondary reports paraphrase Clay as having settled the problem or as listing it as solved; these readings are not supported by the primary text.

Whether Buckmaster and Alpöge’s Euler result is forced: most sources say yes (smooth forcing); one outlet calls it unforced. OpenAI’s Euler result is described as unforced (Santibañez-Leal audit, README summary). The forced and unforced Euler results differ in scope.

Whether the Lean development certifies the natural-language argument. Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen report mismatches at Lemma 8.6 and estimate (10.19). Santibañez-Leal reports that the Lean certificate replays through the kernel. Neither establishes the truth of the theorem or the NL argument. No response from OpenAI to the mismatches was found.

A declaration titled ‘A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics’ (Tao’s blog, 11 Sep 2026; signatories reported as 25 Fields Medallists, one secondary says 28) criticises AI labs using famous open problems as benchmarks. It does not dispute the OpenAI result by name. The Association for Human Mathematics statement (7 Oct 2026, Tao’s blog, opened) rejects OpenAI’s 6 Oct release and urges mathematicians to disengage. Neither is a verification.

summary: Since 26 Jan 2024 the problem has moved in one way that bears directly on the Clay statement. On 8 Sep 2026 OpenAI announced a 166-page manuscript, produced by an unnamed internal multi-agent system (about 10,000 agents over about 88 hours by its account) and formalised in Lean 4, claiming finite-time blow-up of the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations for every viscosity under a smooth external force, on R³ (Clay C) and on the torus (Clay D). I could not open OpenAI’s own announcement (openai.com returns 403) or the manuscript (binary PDF), so the mathematical content rests on the GitHub README read through a fetch, the critiques, Wikipedia, Quanta, Scientific American and the Tao-blog material; the AI details (agent count, hours, cost, messages) are secondary and conflict, and the claim that GPT-6 Astra wrote the Lean formalisation appears only in secondary reports, so I have not entered it in ai.systems. Expert engagement exists but is not verification: Santibañez-Leal (self-published) replayed the Lean development through the kernel and says that does not verify the mathematics; Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen report specific mismatches between the Lean and natural-language arguments (Lemma 8.6, m+4 versus m+5 derivatives, and estimate (10.19)); Duraiswami, a single author, argues the swirl-core geometry does not transfer to the similarity variables; Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol prove a conditional regularity theorem that restricts constructions having two properties they attribute to the OpenAI construction. Cao, Chi and Nie build density results on it (one version withdrawn and restored). I found no qualified referee report, no journal acceptance, and no withdrawal of the OpenAI manuscript. Clay’s 11 Sep 2026 statement says the problem has ‘apparently been settled’ and that evaluation is ‘deliberately unhurried’, and its problem page is still marked Active as I read it. Clay A and B, the unforced questions on R³ and the torus, are not addressed by OpenAI’s claim, and sources read say they remain open; several unforced claims exist (Ri 2025 and 2026, Polozov 2025, Paseva 2025, and Nwankpa 2025 and an Academia.edu item that I could not open), none with public engagement. Neighbouring work includes Hou–Wang–Yang (Sep 2025), a computer-assisted proof of non-uniqueness of unforced Leray–Hopf solutions, which is a different question; Hou’s April 2025 talk (numerical evidence only); the DeepMind unstable-singularity paper (Sep 2025, IPM and bounded Euler); and the 2024 Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa–Zheng hypodissipative result. Buckmaster and Alpöge posted three Lean-formalised forced blow-up papers (IPM, Boussinesq, 3D Euler) on about 7–8 Sep 2026 and an IPM extension on arXiv on 15 Sep, all neighbouring, with LLM assistance; Buckmaster’s statement describes a belief in hypo-dissipative blow-up, not yet released. OpenAI’s 6 Oct release of 700-plus manuscripts (372 problems per Scientific American) is of unknown bearing on Navier–Stokes, and Scientific American reports three of its papers were withdrawn for errors without naming them. Close calls: (a) The bullet names the problem only by title; the Clay statement splits it into four alternatives, and I have listed all four and left the choice to the judging pass. (b) Whether OpenAI’s forced breakdown counts as resolving the bullet depends on that choice; on the Clay wording it answers C and D only. (c) Whether Ri’s H^{1/2} result, if correct, covers Clay A depends on whether smooth finite-energy data lie in H^{1/2} on R³, which appears true but is not stated by the paper. (d) Whether the Clay wording ‘apparently been settled’ is itself a status determination: by its own text it is not.
competing_reading: The stronger reading is that the problem has effectively been settled in the sense the Clay statement anticipates. The claim is a Lean-formalised manuscript; a second party has replayed the Lean development through the kernel; the problem’s own formulator (Fefferman, quoted by Quanta) said he was thrilled the problem was solved; Clay says ‘apparently been settled’; and Wikipedia’s infobox says ‘solution claimed’. On this reading, alternatives C and D are established pending human review, and the record should count the 8 Sep event as a resolution of those alternatives, with A and B the remaining question. The weaker reading is that nothing has been established: the claim is unrefereed; specific Lean-to-natural-language mismatches are reported at named lemmas; the construction’s geometry is contested by a critic; the result concerns forced flows, which the most-discussed version of the problem excludes; Clay has not decided; and the only expert statements are critiques or conditional results.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report or expert verification of the 166-page manuscript, and OpenAI’s answer to the Bastounis et al. examples (Lemma 8.6 and estimate (10.19)). (2) An independent Lean audit of the theorem statements against Clay C and D, with #print axioms showing no sorryAx and a grep of the repository for sorry. (3) The Clay Institute’s own determination under its rules (peer-reviewed publication and a waiting period). (4) For the unforced A and B: any verified proof, or the referee outcome for Ri 2025/2026 and Polozov 2025. (5) For AI attribution: the authors’ own text, in full, on which steps the internal model produced and which humans checked; OpenAI’s blog and manuscript were unreadable to me, so this needs direct access.
